data.title: Apple’s iPhone Duo hits stores with supply short, demand high
data.description:
Since its announcement last month, Apple fans have been eagerly waiting for the release of its newest innovation in years, only for it to instantly sell out in-store

Apple Inc quickly sold out of its limited in-store inventory for the new iPhone Duo, underscoring the strong demand for a foldable device that starts at nearly US$2,000.

The phone went on sale on Friday, bringing back the once-familiar sight of people lining up overnight to get their hands on it first. Marking the company’s most radical reinvention in the iPhone’s nearly two-decade history, the Duo is a major bet that Apple can establish itself in a category that is remained a niche so far.

Apple’s latest gadget packed stores from New York to Beijing and Singapore. The early turnout featured customers collecting their preorders, some trying their luck to secure limited inventory for walk-in purchases, and resellers hoping to flip the devices for a higher price.

In Singapore, a few hundred people stood in line early Friday, including a family of seven from Myanmar who had camped out overnight.

“This is the first true innovation Apple have had in years,” said Peter Ingram, a chief technology officer visiting from London, who plans to buy it upon his return to the UK. “It is expensive. But I tried it out, played with it in the store. It’s incredible how it’s got no crease.”

In the US, Apple stores received about 50 to 200-plus Duo units per location, and they went fast. A store in Los Angeles had no units left for people who arrived after about 6:30am. The 256-gigabyte star white model, priced at US$1,999, was popular with shoppers.

Large crowds on launch day have mostly dissipated in the past few years after Apple, retailers and wireless carriers began maintaining enough inventory to fulfill most orders through home delivery or appointment-based store pickups. However, the company’s first foldable device arrived in much more limited supply.

Consumers placing new orders for the Duo on Apple’s Web site are being offered delivery at the end of January, though some have seen their shipping estimates move up to as soon as next month or December. The delays mark some of the lengthiest for a new Apple product in the company’s modern era.

Shoppers at the Domain Northside Apple Store in Austin were greeted by new chief executive officer John Ternus, who took the helm last month. At the Fifth Avenue location in New York, the line was already stretching multiple blocks at about 5am, three hours before doors opened to iPhone Duo customers. The launch there was marked by Apple’s senior vice president of marketing Greg Joswiak, and vice president of retail stores Vanessa Trigub.

At the Apple Store in Lawrence Township, New Jersey, about 64km outside Philadelphia, the 256 and 512-gigabyte configurations sold out within the first half hour, leaving the pricier 1 and 2-terabyte (TB) models.

Victor Osorio, a shopper at that location, said even though foldables are not new, “Apple always does something different and adds extra spice to it. I’m not nervous about the form factor but I am about the hinge. I don’t want it to get in the way but it looks OK so far.” Osorio arrived early with his partner, Victoria, who also purchased the Duo and said she was intrigued by the device’s multitasking capabilities.

At the same location, Naveed Abubacker said he trades in his iPhone every year. “Foldable technology has been around for a while and Apple is late to the gate but I’m ready for it,” he said. “If it doesn’t work out for me, I’ll return it.”

In China, Shanghai and Beijing saw a moderate turnout, with most Duo buyers already loyal Apple customers who said they were excited to try out the new design. Many had to register in advance to secure their unit.

“It will take some getting used to,” Andy Shen said at Apple’s Sanlitun store in Beijing. “I chose the Duo mainly because it opens up to a bigger screen to enable better experience with videos, though its other functions are not measuring up to earlier generations, like the camera.”

As one of the most expensive mainstream smartphones ever sold, the Duo had raised questions about just how much demand there would be. Most of the shoppers in Beijing and Singapore looked past the high price and focused on the promise of a truly new Apple product after many years of iterative updates.

The iPhone lineup is Apple’s largest moneymaker, generating about half of the company’s revenue. And the Duo is the biggest single design change in the device’s nearly history. Although the company was not first to market with a foldable phone, it looks to gain an edge with a more polished product built for Apple fans.

Rather than a repeat of the lackluster debut of the Vision Pro headset nearly three years ago, the Duo’s launch is shaping up to be a throwback to the iPhone introductions of old — when demand far outstripped supply. That is the case even with device prices reaching as high as US$3,199 for models with 2TB of storage.

Although the Duo’s cost sets a record for a mass-market smartphone, Apple’s competitors such as Samsung Electronics Co, Xiaomi Corp and Oppo have been raising prices as well. Shortages of memory chips and other components have made consumer electronics more expensive across the board.

The new phones from Apple are difficult to produce because of their advanced hinge and new display technology. They are also only built in a limited number of facilities in China. Apple expanded production in the past few years for its traditional iPhones, including to India, which has helped with supply.

Apple reports its quarterly earnings results on Nov. 2, but those would not include sales of the Duo because the period concluded at the end of last month. It would reflect early sales of iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max models, which debuted on Sept. 18.

Other new versions, such as the entry-level iPhone or the updated Air, would not go on sale until next year, Bloomberg News reported. That marks a change in the company’s usual release schedule, a move meant to help spread out revenue across the year.

data.title: The last reliable luxury shoppers are retreating in mainland China
data.description:
Luxury powerhouses including Hermes and Cartier are suffering steeper slumps in China, in a sign that a spending pullback by the country’s wealthy consumers is hitting even the most resilient brands.

Sales at the brands in mainland China fell as much as double-digits in August and last month compared to the same period a year ago, two research firms surveyed by Bloomberg that track industry data said. The drop is significant as Hermes International SCA and Cie Financiere Richemont SA’s Cartier had been relatively unaffected in the country as a broader slowdown in luxury consumption took hold in June, the firms’ data show.

Mainland sales for the 25 largest luxury labels including Louis Vuitton and Gucci have also contracted further, plunging by double-digits in August and last month, the firms said.

Business remained weak during China’s National Day holiday, a seven-day break early this month dubbed the golden week, even as consumers spent more on travel, according to people familiar with the matter who asked not to be identified because they are not authorized to speak publicly. Some executives at major luxury houses now fear the slump could become more widespread and persist until next year, the people said.

Concerns are mounting as Beijing’s widening scrutiny of offshore wealth and a cooling artificial intelligence stock rally rattle private fortunes, testing the long-held belief that the luxury industry’s wealthiest clients are largely recession-proof. Global brands had long banked on these top-tier spenders as China’s middle-class retreated during a prolonged property-market slump and wider economic slowdown. Now, they are facing the possibility of their key customers and aspirational shoppers spending less at the same time.

“The recurring message from our annual Asia consumer and luxury trip over the past three years was that conditions were difficult, but that ‘next year would be better,’” HSBC Holdings PLC analyst Anne-Laure Bismuth said in a note this month. “This time, however, meetings in Hong Kong, Xiamen and Shanghai provided no timeline or evidence of a recovery in Chinese luxury consumption.”

Hermes and Cartier did not respond to requests for comment.

Resilient demand from other parts of Greater China, including Hong Kong and Macau, has helped offset some of the declines in the mainland for high-end jewelry brands such as Cartier, research firm JL Warren said. Still, the weakness in one of the luxury group’s largest markets has weighed on their earnings.

Hermes on Thursday reported flat sales in Asia-Pacific for the third quarter. Revenue in the region excluding Japan fell short of analyst expectations for 1.55 percent growth.

The performance in the region — which includes China and accounts for about 42 percent of Hermes’ total revenue — is a sign that the Birkin bag maker is not immune to the spending curbs affecting Chinese shoppers.

China’s macroeconomic environment remains challenging, compounded by sluggish financial markets and ongoing tax-related campaigns, Hermes chief financial officer Eric Du Halgouet said during a post-earnings briefing.

LVMH Moet Hennessy Louis Vuitton SE’s third-quarter results showed a double-digit drop in domestic China sales amid a trademark controversy involving its largest brand Louis Vuitton. Purchases by Chinese shoppers overseas also fell by a mid-single-digit percentage. The weakness contributed to a 5 percent revenue slump in Asia excluding Japan, the group’s only region to post a negative performance.

Gucci sales fell 6 percent in the third quarter, worse than analysts’ expectations, hurt by weak consumption in China. That has contributed to parent Kering SA’s quarterly decline.

Amid the broader economic downturn, Chinese consumers have become more selective about discretionary spending, prioritizing travel, dining and other experiences over highly visible luxury purchases. Even among those still willing to spend, tastes have shifted. Many younger shoppers are gravitating away from prominent logos and status-driven purchases in favor of understated products that emphasize craftsmanship and quality, fueling the rise of so-called “quiet luxury.”

Retail sales growth in August slowed further to 0.4 percent before improving last month. Big-ticket items including jewelry and cars performed the worst, plunging as much as 21 percent in business receipts in the two months.

Comparisons are likely to become less challenging next year after a steep downturn this year, potentially helping major luxury groups return to reported growth, Shanghai-based consultancy Foresight Performance Partners co-founder Jacques Roizen said. However, any improvement in headline numbers is unlikely to signal a meaningful recovery in demand, he said.

“Beneath those comparisons is a structural problem,” Roizen said. “Much of the aspirational middle-class has moved away from luxury, while wealthier consumers have become more cautious. The underlying pressures are unlikely to change quickly.”

data.title: There is no escaping tech tycoon villains (at the movies)
data.description:
There is a striking moment near the end of Musk, a new documentary by Oscar-winning filmmaker Alex Gibney, when the world’s richest man is asked why he considers it important to develop X into what he calls a global platform for collective consciousness.

“I guess ...” Elon Musk replies to his questioner, the billionaire Indian entrepreneur Nikhil Kamath, before his voice trails off. There is a pause of several seconds in which neither man says anything. Eventually, after a couple of false starts, Musk settles on: “To increase our understanding of the universe.”

The exchange — originally broadcast as part of Kamath’s People by WTF podcast in November last year — stands out because it follows more than three and a half hours of a film in which Musk is rarely short of words or solutions. We see his early successes during the dot-com boom, followed by his stewardship of Tesla Inc and SpaceX, the acquisition of Twitter and, ultimately, his alliance with US President Donald Trump.

At every step, Gibney depicts Musk as relentlessly accumulating money and power, shrugging off a string of controversies — business and personal — along the way. The section on the Department of Government Efficiency, the Trump administration initiative ostensibly created to identify and cut waste, is especially troubling to watch, particularly when it focuses on cuts to the US Agency for International Development and their impact on projects in Africa. However, when asked to articulate his deeper purpose, the tycoon is lost for words.

Musk represents a prominent example of a shift in contemporary cinema: While multibillionaire tech tycoons have made for convenient villains in the past, recent portrayals are more frequent and less ambivalent. Gibney, 72 — a prolific filmmaker who won the 2007 Academy Award for best documentary feature for Taxi to the Dark Side about abuse by US soldiers — paints a picture of ruthlessness, cynicism and a chronic lack of regulatory oversight. Musk is designed to leave the viewer feeling bleak about the world. As Gibney asks by way of a mission statement: “How could Musk assume so much power, and why had we given it to him?”

That question, to which there is no straightforward answer, speaks to a growing sense of public discomfort with the way superrich tech leaders and their companies have come to dominate the corporate, political and media landscape — as well as our personal lives. The release of Musk came just months after its subject became the world’s first trillionaire following SpaceX’s record-breaking initial public offering, an unheard-of level of wealth that is helping to fund Republican campaigns ahead of the Nov. 3 midterm elections. According to a Pew survey conducted last year, more than half of Americans have an unfavorable view of Musk, while two-thirds had a negative perception of Meta Platforms Inc chief executive officer Mark Zuckerberg.

Another version of Elon Musk appears in Artificial which screened at this month’s London Film Festival ahead of its release this winter. The film, directed by Luca Guadagnino, charts the early years of OpenAI, which Musk co-founded in 2015. Musk left the company in 2018 and has tried unsuccessfully to sue its present incarnation, allowing writer Simon Rich to make the film version played by Ike Barinholtz a form of comic relief — all facial tics and self-importance — rather than anything more sinister.

The role of tech tycoon villain instead goes to Andrew Garfield, who plays OpenAI CEO Sam Altman. The film portrays him as the ultra-ambitious and unscrupulous driving force behind the company that gave us ChatGPT, with the movie’s conscience represented by co-founder and chief scientist Ilya Sutskever (played by Yura Borisov — best known as the kind-hearted henchman in Anora).

Artificial goes on to tell the story of Altman and Sutskever’s eventual falling-out, with Altman fired and swiftly reinstated with the support of Microsoft Corp, OpenAI’s main investor. Garfield plays Altman as increasingly cold and manipulative, swatting aside any concerns about AI safety and the people who get in his way. “I didn’t invent teen suicide!” he yells at one fellow executive, when warned of ChatGPT’s darker potential.

Facebook founder Zuckerberg was the subject of David Fincher’s acclaimed 2010 movie The Social Network and it feels apt that writer Aaron Sorkin should return with a de facto sequel some 16 years later.

In the original movie, the action revolves around a litigation against Zuckerberg during Facebook’s early years. In this fall’s The Social Reckoning he is now well-established — and it is Wall Street Journal reporter Jeff Horwitz (Jeremy Allen White) and Facebook employee-turned-whistleblower Frances Haugen (Mikey Madison) who are out to get him.

The story shows how the duo worked together on Horwitz’s award-winning reporting on Facebook and its algorithm in 2021, with a particular focus on how users can become radicalized and pushed toward extremist groups.

The rather unsubtle point of The Social Reckoning is that Facebook and Zuckerberg are terrible, while journalists and whistleblowers are good. It was not as binary when Sorkin was writing The Social Network, where the Facebook founder could be seen as a misfit simply trying to get his own back on the alpha males and women he believed looked down on him.

Some might see Facebook as a product of the past, with the stakes around the technology developed by OpenAI and rival Anthropic PBC much higher. The drunk woman who delivers a racist diatribe at police officers at the start of The Social Reckoning — radicalized by Facebook, Haugen deduces — might seem trivial compared with the potential for AI to overpower humanity, as is threatened in Artificial.

The power of technology to turn people against each other, only for us all to be overpowered by robots, drives the fear coursing through all these films. “We’ll have to build a bunker,” Geoffrey Hinton (Mark Rylance), Sutskever’s early mentor, warns him early in Artificial. “And hide from the Terminator.”

data.title: Young Optics expects shipments drop
data.description:
SOFT DEMAND: Shipments of optical components rose quarter-on-quarter on AR glasses production, while 3D printing product shipments slowed, the company said

Camera lens supplier Young Optics Inc (揚明光學) yesterday said it expects shipments this quarter to decline sequentially due to soft demand, partly because customers’ planned changes to new logistics projection lenses could delay or suspend demand.

Shipments of 3D printing products this quarter are expected to increase slightly as customers begin testing new models, Young Optics said in a statement to the Taiwan Stock Exchange.

Shipments from other product lines are expected to remain flat or decline slightly from last quarter as customers become more cautious about year-end inventory management, the company said.

Young Optics yesterday posted a second consecutive quarterly decline in net profit of NT$1.22 million (US$37,529) last quarter, slumping 76.25 percent from NT$5.14 million the previous quarter. That represented an improvement from a net loss of NT$10.08 million a year earlier, company data showed.

Earnings per share were NT$0.01, down from NT$0.05 the previous quarter, but up from losses per share of NT$0.09 a year earlier.

Gross margin rose to 16.8 percent last quarter from 16.44 percent in the second quarter, but was down from 17.02 percent a year earlier.

In the third quarter, shipments of smart home products were flat from the previous quarter as continued growth in new models shipments was offset by the phaseout of older low-end lens products, Young Optics said.

Shipments of optical components increased quarter-on-quarter as customers’ new augmented reality (AR) glasses entered mass production, while 3D printing product shipments slowed as customers adjusted inventories of older models and conducted verification of new models, it said.

Automotive product shipments increased slightly as new lidar lens models entered mass production and replaced older models, the company added.

The third-quarter shipment trends largely matched the guidance provided in July.

In the second quarter, automotive products accounted for about 15 to 20 percent of Young Optics’ NT$738.28 million in revenue, while optical components made up 25 to 30 percent, company president Cynthia Chang (張雅容) said at the time.

The share of optical components could rise to about 30 percent this year, supported by volume production of logistics projection lenses and AR glasses, Chang said.

Regarding fiber array unit products, the company said two mechanical transfer ferrule projects are undergoing trial production, while molded glass lens arrays and optical transceiver modules remain in the proof-of-concept verification phase, Young Optics said.

The company is also developing new automotive lidar lens products, Young Optics said.

Increases in manufacturing complexity, particularly in molded glass components, could weigh on gross margin during the initial stage of mass production, it said.

Young Optics has three major customers for applications related to AR glasses, mainly supplying optical engine components, said Wayne Lin (林威嶧), another company president.

One customer focuses primarily on swimming goggles, while the others are leading North American customers for AR glasses, Lin said.

One of the two North American customers is already in mass production, while the other began mass production last year and plans to launch a second-generation product in the second half of this year, he said.

data.title: US moots curbs on funds to Chinese biotech firms
data.description:
The administration of US President Donald Trump is seeking to restrict investment in Chinese biotechnology companies, potentially complicating financial ties at a time when US drugmakers are increasingly turning to China for new medicines.

The US Department of the Treasury on Thursday proposed adding biotechnology to a list of sensitive technologies subject to investment limits involving foreign adversaries, citing national security concerns.

The proposed regulations would require US investors to notify Washington about some transactions involving foreign companies developing sensitive technologies and prohibit others entirely.

The rules would expand a program targeting investments in areas including artificial intelligence, semiconductors and quantum computing.

The move represents the latest escalation in Washington’s efforts to rein in China’s biotech advances.

Last year, the US Congress passed the Biosecure Act to restrict federal agencies and government-funded companies from using or procuring services from designated Chinese biotech firms, although the restrictions were weaker and narrower than initially proposed.

The US tightening comes as Beijing is also adjusting its own approach.

In a sign of biotechnology’s growing strategic importance, China last week proposed adding several biomedical technologies to its export-control list — although its plan explicitly allows licensing deals for drugs to continue.

Chinese biotechnology companies have become a source of innovation for the pharmaceutical industry. US drugmakers are increasingly turning to China to license promising treatments as they search for new products to replenish their pipelines.

Licensing deals are not expressly prohibited under Washington’s proposed rules, according to Duane Wright, senior healthcare policy analyst at Bloomberg Intelligence.

Wright said that the Treasury Department proposal begins with a “very broad definition” of biotechnology — covering small molecules, biologics, vaccines and cell and gene therapies — but leaves room to narrow the pharmaceutical provisions after stakeholder comments.

data.title: September industrial production rises 19 percent
data.description:
STREAK OF 31 MONTHS: Consumer electronics launched by global brands boosted the information and electronic components industries, the economy ministry said

Industrial production rose more than 19 percent year-on-year last month, driven by the artificial intelligence (AI) boom, marking the 31st consecutive month of growth, the Ministry of Economic Affairs said yesterday.

The industrial production index rose 19.17 percent from a year earlier to 140.76 last month, while the manufacturing subindex, which accounts for more than 90 percent of total production, rose 20.21 percent to 143.31, ministry data showed.

In the third quarter, industrial production rose 21.95 percent year-on-year, with the manufacturing subindex up 23.05 percent, while in the first nine months of the year, industrial production grew 20.53 percent, with the manufacturing subindex up 21.83 percent, the data showed.

The export-oriented manufacturing sector continued to benefit from strong global demand for AI applications, high-performance computing devices and cloud services, the ministry said in a statement.

Launches of new consumer electronics by international brands also boosted Taiwan’s information and electronic components industries, while also lifting non-tech manufacturers, the statement said.

Last month, production in the electronic components industry rose 23.62 percent year-on-year, led by 12-inch wafer foundries, integrated circuit (IC) packaging and testing firms, memorychip suppliers, IC designers and IC substrate makers, it said.

Production in the computer, electronic and optical products industry soared 45.92 percent last month from a year earlier as AI development pushed up demand for AI servers, switches, semiconductor inspection equipment and solid-state drives, the statement said.

That marked the 39th straight month of growth, the ministry said.

With semiconductor suppliers installing equipment to expand capacity, production in the machinery industry rose 26.02 percent year-on-year, while base metal production rose 1.39 percent on a recovery in demand, it said.

Bucking the trend, production in the chemical material and fertilizer industry fell 4.29 percent year-on-year due to slower demand and reduced output during annual maintenance, it said.

Production of autos and auto parts rose 2.35 percent year-on-year, driven by higher output of electric passenger cars and all-terrain vehicles, it said.

Looking ahead, the global AI boom and year-end holiday shopping season are expected to continue supporting Taiwan’s industrial production for the rest of the year, although geopolitical tensions and major economies’ trade policies could continue to create uncertainty for the global economy, the ministry said.

Manufacturing production is expected to expand by 20.5 to 24.2 percent year-on-year this month, it added.

data.title: SK Hynix cancels IPO of Solidigm unit
data.description:
SK Hynix Inc yesterday scrapped plans for a potential US$10 billion US listing of its Solidigm unit after facing strong opposition from regulators and shareholders, becoming the latest firm to pull an initial public offering (IPO) while growing investor unease over the artificial intelligence (AI) boom rocks markets.

The retreat followed domestic regulatory scrutiny over concerns that Solidigm’s IPO could dilute share value for minority investors and complicate SK Group’s ownership structure. The South Korean chipmaker, which also halted discussions around pre-IPO investment, in a regulatory filing cited “recent capital market conditions.”

Solidigm, one of the world’s largest makers of flash memory critical to storage in data centers, is the latest high-profile firm to suspend or cancel an IPO. It joins data center developers Firmus Grid Ltd and AirTrunk in pulling back at a time fears of an AI bubble are roiling global markets.

However, in SK Hynix’s case, the withdrawal was driven largely by regulatory opposition in South Korea.

The controversy over Solidigm had become a test of Seoul’s efforts to improve corporate governance and minority shareholder protections — addressing the country’s chronic equity undervaluation, known as the “Korea discount.”

The decision is “a major positive for [South] Korean corporate governance,” said Ryan Albert, founder and managing member of Terton Capital. “Shareholders, governance groups and the regulator all weighed in, identifying the core conflict of the group keeping control of Solidigm.”

After the announcement, SK Hynix’s shares rose, defying a broad market slide triggered by a rout in US technology stocks. They had plunged about 60 percent from their June peak, battered by worries over slowing memorychip demand exacerbated by dilution fears.

The company in July completed the biggest-ever US listing by a foreign company, raising US$26.5 billion.

Solidigm had already picked banks including Goldman Sachs Group Inc and Morgan Stanley to work on the offering, looking to raise about US$10 billion, people familiar with the matter have said.

It planned to list as soon as next year, in a deal that would have valued the company at as much as US$100 billion, Bloomberg News has reported.

The market value of SK Hynix’s Seoul-listed shares is about US$679 billion, about half of their June peak.

SK Hynix at the time said that Solidigm was reviewing options to improve its business competitiveness. Now, the company sought to reassure investors that the decision to pull the deal does not reflect changes in the unit’s growth prospects or investment needs.

“In light of recent capital market conditions and share price trends, Solidigm determined that it was necessary to reassess whether an IPO would be the most beneficial option for SK Hynix and its existing shareholders at this time,” the company said in a statement.

The reversal follows concerns by South Korean regulators that the planned offering could amount to a duplicate listing.

Fibonacci Asset Management Global chief executive officer Jung In-yun said that the cancelation was positive for SK Hynix shareholders because it would ease concerns about dilution of the parent company’s economic interest in Solidigm, and the valuation discount associated with listing both a parent and its subsidiary.

data.title: Manufacturing sentiment rises to a 55-month high
data.description:
Business sentiment in the export-oriented manufacturing sector rose to its highest level in 55 months last month, buoyed by the global artificial intelligence (AI) boom, the Taiwan Institute of Economic Research (TIER, 台經院) said yesterday, while warning of potential risks ahead.

The manufacturing sector’s composite index, which gauges business sentiment among local manufacturers, rose 0.50 points from August to 101.39, its highest level since February 2022, data compiled by TIER showed.

The composite index for the service sector fell 3.15 points month-on-month to 92.65, while the index for the construction industry rebounded from a previous decline, rising 2.81 points from August to 110.42, the data showed.

TIER, one of Taiwan’s leading economic think tanks, said that manufacturers continued to benefit from massive global investments in AI infrastructure and inventory buildup by international brands ahead of new product launches, including the iPhone 18 series and iPhone Duo.

A surge in international crude oil prices also pushed up the prices of petrochemical products, while the completion of annual maintenance by some non-tech industries helped boost production, the institute said.

In TIER’s survey last month, 26.8 percent of manufacturing respondents said business conditions had improved that month, up from 19.5 percent in August, while 20.3 percent said conditions had worsened, down from 25.6 percent a month earlier.

However, expectations for the next six months weakened.

In the survey, 24.0 percent of respondents expected business conditions to improve, down 3.1 percentage points from August, while 19.8 percent expected them to deteriorate, up 1.8 percentage points.

Gordon Sun (孫明德), director of TIER’s Economic Forecasting Center, said that despite support from the AI boom and the peak season for consumer electronics, Taiwan’s economy still faced risks, including the possibility of the US Federal Reserve taking a more hawkish stance to curb inflation.

A Fed rate hike would likely strengthen the US dollar against the Taiwan dollar, potentially prompting foreign institutional investors to pull funds out of Taiwan and causing volatility in local financial markets, Sun said.

Military conflicts in the Middle East could push crude oil prices higher and prompt upstream petrochemical suppliers to raise prices, although such increases could weaken demand from downstream buyers, Sun said.

Sun also noted concerns about a possible slowdown in AI development, which have recently weighed on global stock markets.

In the service sector, recent financial market volatility has made businesses more cautious, although the food and beverage industry continued to benefit from rising demand, TIER said.

In construction, easing of selective credit controls in the middle of last month by Taiwan’s central bank supported the property market, but the industry still faces a large inventory of unsold homes, the think tank said.

data.title: Opening up
data.description: People stand near a display of Apple Inc iPhone Duos at the Apple Store in Covent Garden, London, yesterday. For Apple, the iPhone Duo is one of the first major product debuts under new chief executive officer John Ternus, who took the helm last month amid a flurry of announcements that has included the HomeView smart home hub and AirPods 5.

data.title: Four financial firms approve merger
data.description:
SHARE SWAP: First Securities Investment Trust Co would be the surviving entity due to its larger asset base and stronger operating performance, executives said

Four state-owned financial holding companies yesterday approved a plan to merge their investment trust subsidiaries into a larger, more competitive asset manager, aiming to cut operating costs, broaden product offerings and improve Taiwan’s position as a regional asset management hub.

The planned merger aims to achieve economies of scale by pooling resources, technology and distribution networks, allowing the combined company to improve operating efficiency and compete more effectively, executives said.

First Financial Holding Co (第一金控), Mega Financial Holding Co (兆豐金控), Taiwan Cooperative Financial Holding Co (合庫金控) and Hua Nan Financial Holdings Co (華南金控) said their boards and those of their investment trust subsidiaries had approved the deal.

First Securities Investment Trust Co (第一金投信) would be the surviving entity because of its larger asset base and stronger operating performance, they said.

The merger, which requires regulatory approval, is planned for Jan. 1, 2028.

First Securities Investment Trust would absorb Mega International Investment Trust Co (兆豐國際投信), Taiwan Cooperative Securities Investment Trust Co (合作金庫投信) and Hua Nan Investment Trust Co (華南永昌投信), with all of the approximately 370 employees to have the option to stay on.

The parent companies would hold stakes of 50.3 percent, 30.4 percent, 9.8 percent and 9.5 percent respectively in the combined firm.

The transaction would be conducted through a share swap, with First Securities Investment Trust issuing about 59.3 million new common shares.

The new company would retain the First Securities Investment Trust name, with First Financial controlling appointments to its top management positions, First Financial Holding president Frank Fang (方螢基) said.

The combined company is expected to benefit from lower operating costs and more effective use of the four groups’ distribution networks, Fang said, adding that a broader range of investment products should help improve profitability and shareholder returns.

First Securities Investment Trust president Richard Kao (高子敬) said that the entity’s assets under management would total about NT$500 billion (US$15.38 billion), including publicly offered funds and discretionary investment mandates.

The company aims to increase assets in publicly offered funds by 15 percent annually and those in discretionary investment mandates by 10 percent, Kao said.

To achieve those targets, it plans to develop products focused on retirement planning, sustainable investment, overseas asset allocation and wealthy clients, he said, adding that it intends to pursue opportunities arising from the government’s push to establish Taiwan as an Asian asset management hub.

The combined publicly offered fund assets of the four merging firms would rank about 12th among Taiwan’s investment trust firms and the merged entity would aim to break into the top 10, he said.

The merged company would have seven directors and two supervisors.

First Financial would appoint four directors and one supervisor, while each of the other three financial holding companies would appoint one director.

Mega Financial would appoint one supervisor.

The four merging companies pledged to protect employee and customer rights during the integration.

First Securities Investment Trust would assume responsibility for existing customers, whose rights would remain protected under applicable regulations.
